title: Why can random UUIDv4 primary keys cause index fragmentation and slower inserts versus auto-increment, and how do time-ordered IDs (UUIDv7 / ULID) fix this while staying globally unique?
shortTitle: Why can random UUIDv4 primary keys cause index fragmentation and slower inserts, and how do time-ordered IDs fix this

s1_definition.profdef: A UUIDv4 is a fully random 128-bit identifier, so consecutive inserts land at random positions in the primary-key B-tree. This causes page splits, poor cache locality, and index fragmentation, and in clustered engines it also scatters the physical row data, making inserts slower and tables larger. Auto-increment keys always append to the rightmost page, keeping the tree dense and insert-friendly. Time-ordered identifiers like UUIDv7 and ULID embed a leading timestamp so new values are monotonically increasing and also append near the right edge, restoring insert locality while remaining globally unique and coordination-free.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine the National Bank of India files new account folders into a cabinet that must stay in sorted order. With auto-increment numbers, every new folder goes neatly at the very back — fast and tidy. With random UUIDv4 numbers, each new folder must be jammed into a random spot in the middle of the cabinet, forcing the clerk to shove existing folders aside to make room (a page split), and the cabinet ends up full of half-empty, messy drawers (fragmentation). A time-ordered UUIDv7 is like a number that starts with today's timestamp, so new folders again cluster near the back in time order, keeping the cabinet tidy, while still being globally unique.
s1_definition.oneliner: Random UUIDv4 scatters inserts across the B-tree causing splits and fragmentation; time-ordered UUIDv7 or ULID keeps inserts near the right edge like auto-increment, while staying globally unique.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A UUIDv4 is a fully random 128-bit identifier, so consecutive inserts land at random positions in the primary-key B-tree. This causes page splits, poor cache locality, and index fragmentation, and in clustered engines it also scatters the physical row data, making inserts slower and tables larger. Auto-increment keys always append to the rightmost page, keeping the tree dense and insert-friendly. Time-ordered identifiers like UUIDv7 and ULID embed a leading timestamp so new values are monotonically increasing and also append near the right edge, restoring insert locality while remaining globally unique and coordination-free.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine the National Bank of India files new account folders into a cabinet that must stay in sorted order. With auto-increment numbers, every new folder goes neatly at the very back — fast and tidy. With random UUIDv4 numbers, each new folder must be jammed into a random spot in the middle of the cabinet, forcing the clerk to shove existing folders aside to make room (a page split), and the cabinet ends up full of half-empty, messy drawers (fragmentation). A time-ordered UUIDv7 is like a number that starts with today's timestamp, so new folders again cluster near the back in time order, keeping the cabinet tidy, while still being globally unique.

**One line to remember:** Random UUIDv4 scatters inserts across the B-tree causing splits and fragmentation; time-ordered UUIDv7 or ULID keeps inserts near the right edge like auto-increment, while staying globally unique.

sections.s2_technical:
A primary-key index is a B-tree kept in sorted key order. With auto-increment, each new key is larger than all previous ones, so it always lands on the rightmost leaf page. That page fills up and a fresh page is appended — a cheap, sequential operation with excellent cache locality and almost no wasted space.

A UUIDv4 is random across its whole range, so each new key is equally likely to belong anywhere in the tree. The engine must find the correct leaf for a random key, and if that leaf is full it performs a page split: it allocates a new page and moves roughly half the entries over. Random inserts cause frequent page splits all over the tree, which fragments the index into many partly-filled pages, wastes space, and hurts cache hit rates because the working set is spread across far more pages than necessary.

In a clustered engine like InnoDB this is worse, because the primary key dictates the physical row order. Random primary keys scatter the actual row data too, so inserts touch random disk pages and the table itself becomes fragmented. On top of that, InnoDB stores the primary key inside every secondary index, so a 16-byte random key bloats every secondary index compared to a 4 or 8 byte integer.

Time-ordered identifiers fix the root cause. UUIDv7 places a 48-bit Unix-millisecond timestamp in the high bits, so values generated over time are approximately monotonically increasing. ULID does the same with a 48-bit timestamp plus random suffix. Because the leading bits increase with time, new keys again land near the right edge of the tree, inserts become close to sequential, page splits drop sharply, and fragmentation largely disappears — all while keeping global uniqueness and needing no central coordinator. A senior nuance: store these as a compact 16-byte binary type or native uuid, not as a 36-character string, because the string form triples storage and defeats much of the benefit; and remember the timestamp prefix means the id leaks creation time, so it is an identifier, not a secret.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The payments team switched transaction primary keys from auto-increment to random UUIDv4 for distributed generation, and insert throughput dropped while the index bloated. This is exactly the random-insert fragmentation problem.

Problem 2 — They needed globally unique ids generated across many services without a central sequence, but they also needed insert locality back. This is exactly what UUIDv7 provides: unique, coordination-free, and time-ordered.

Problem 3 — An early attempt stored UUIDs as CHAR(36) and saw little improvement. This is exactly the storage nuance: the id must be stored as 16-byte binary.

The mini-project builds a transaction service that generates UUIDv7 keys, stores them compactly, and inserts in approximate time order, with logging that shows the monotonic prefix keeping inserts near the right edge.

sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Build and run
mvn clean package -DskipTests
java -jar target/uuid-key-service-1.0.0.jar --spring.profiles.active=dev

# UUIDv7 ids are near-sorted; successive values share the timestamp prefix
psql -d bankdb -c "SELECT txn_id FROM transactions ORDER BY created_at LIMIT 5;"

# Measure index bloat (should stay low with time-ordered keys)
psql -d bankdb -c "SELECT pg_size_pretty(pg_relation_size('transactions_pkey'));"
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: two transactions recorded a few milliseconds apart for account SAV2001.

Step 1 — The service calls the UUIDv7 generator. It reads the current time in milliseconds and places those 48 bits at the front of the 16-byte identifier, then fills the rest with random bits and stamps the version and variant markers.

Step 2 — Because the two transactions are recorded milliseconds apart, their identifiers share almost the entire leading timestamp and differ only in the low random bits, so the second id sorts just after the first.

Step 3 — The insert goes into the primary-key B-tree. Since each new key is larger than recent ones, it lands on or near the rightmost leaf page, exactly like auto-increment, so the page fills sequentially and rarely splits.

Step 4 — The row is stored as a compact 16-byte native uuid, not a 36-character string, so the key stays small, the index stays dense, and in a clustered engine the physical rows also cluster near the right edge instead of scattering.

Step 5 — Over millions of inserts the index remains dense with little fragmentation, insert throughput stays high, and the ids are still globally unique and generated without any central coordinator — the best of both worlds.

```text
2026-10-25 15:42:12 INFO  TransactionService - Recorded txn 018f2a1c-... for SAV2001 amount 50000 (UUIDv7 time-ordered, low fragmentation)
2026-10-25 15:42:12 INFO  TransactionService - Recorded txn 018f2a1c-... for SAV2001 amount 25000 (UUIDv7 time-ordered, low fragmentation)
```


sections.s6_takeaway:
Random UUIDv4 primary keys cause problems because a primary-key index is a B-tree kept in sorted order, and a fully random key is equally likely to belong anywhere in that tree. So every insert targets a random leaf page, and when that page is full the engine performs a page split, moving half the entries to a new page. Random inserts trigger frequent splits all over the tree, which leaves it fragmented with many half-empty pages, wastes space, and ruins cache locality. In a clustered engine like InnoDB it is worse, because the primary key also dictates the physical row order, so the actual data scatters too, and the 16-byte random key bloats every secondary index that embeds it.

Auto-increment avoids all of this because each new key is larger than the last, so it always appends to the rightmost page — dense, sequential, and cheap. The catch is that auto-increment needs a central database sequence, which is awkward in distributed systems. Time-ordered identifiers like UUIDv7 and ULID solve both sides: they put a 48-bit millisecond timestamp in the high bits, so new values are approximately monotonically increasing and land near the right edge of the tree just like auto-increment, while still being globally unique and generated with no central coordinator.

At the National Bank of India our payments team moved transaction keys to random UUIDv4 for distributed generation and saw insert throughput fall and the index bloat badly. I switched them to UUIDv7, which kept the global uniqueness and coordination-free generation they needed but restored insert locality, so page splits dropped and fragmentation largely disappeared. Crucially I also made sure we stored the id as a native 16-byte uuid rather than a 36-character string, because an early attempt stored it as CHAR(36) and tripled the key size, which had defeated most of the benefit.

The nuance I close with is that the timestamp prefix means a UUIDv7 leaks its creation time, so it is an identifier, never a secret or an authentication token, and I always verify the improvement by measuring index size and insert latency before and after the change.
